title: PLL Nonidealities and Jitter
intro: Imperfections of the PFD and charge pump that disturb the control voltage in lock, and how a PLL passes or rejects jitter (Razavi, Section 16.3).

blocks.text: Dead zone and why reset pulses help

Imagine a PFD that produced no pulses at all at zero phase error. For a tiny error it would produce pulses so narrow that, with finite rise and fall times, they never reach a logic level and never turn on the pump switches. Below some error $\phi_0$ the pump does nothing, the loop gain is zero, and the VCO phase drifts freely inside $\pm\phi_0$: a dead zone, seen as jitter on the output.

blocks.alt: Charge pump average current against phase error: zero over a band from minus phi0 to plus phi0, then rising linearly on each side; a dashed straight line through the origin shows the ideal.
blocks.caption: A dead zone around zero phase error.

blocks.text: The PFD's coincident reset pulses fix this: at zero error both UP and DOWN are on for $T_P \approx 5$ gate delays, long enough to switch the pump fully, so any small extra error simply makes one pulse slightly longer and the net current changes in proportion.
A transistor-level pump uses current sources M1 (NMOS) and M2 (PMOS) with switches M3, M4; UP must be inverted to drive the PMOS switch.

items: Skew between UP and DOWN: if one switch turns on before the other, the net current briefly jumps to $\pm I_P$ every cycle. A transmission gate in the non-inverted path equalizes the delays.

Current mismatch: if $I_1 \ne I_2$, the overlap pulse leaves net charge each cycle. The loop responds by settling at a phase error that makes the net charge per cycle zero: a static phase offset, still with periodic ripple. Low $r_o$ in short-channel devices makes the mismatch depend on $V_{cont}$, and switch charge injection and feedthrough add to both.

Charge sharing: while the switches are off, node X (above the NMOS source) is pulled to ground and node Y to $V_{DD}$. When they close, these capacitances share charge with $C_P$, and since X and Y move by different amounts (depending on $V_{cont}$), $V_{cont}$ jumps. Bootstrapping fixes it: a unity-gain buffer holds X and Y at $V_{cont}$ through extra switches whenever the main switches are open.

blocks.text: For a DOWN current larger than UP by $\Delta I$ and overlap $T_P$, zero net charge requires UP to start earlier by $\Delta t$ with $I_P\Delta t = \Delta I\,T_P$:
The PLL Building Blocks chapter turns these effects into numbers: the static phase offset from mismatch, reference spurs from mismatch and leakage, and the circuits that fix them.

A jittery waveform has zero crossings displaced from where a perfect period would put them; equivalently its excess phase $\phi_n(t)$ wanders: $x(t) = A\cos[\omega t + \phi_n(t)]$. How fast it wanders matters as much as how far. Two sources matter in a PLL:

items: Input jitter: the closed-loop $H(s)$ is low-pass, so slow input jitter passes to the output and fast jitter is filtered.
VCO jitter: with the input clean, the transfer from VCO phase noise to the output is high-pass:

blocks.text: Slow VCO drift (temperature, for instance) produces a slowly growing phase error that the loop corrects; fast VCO noise is not caught before it appears. The loop bandwidth is chosen according to which source is worse: a clean reference and a noisy VCO (rings) want a wide loop; a jittery input with a good VCO wants a narrow one.

blocks.alt: Two curves against log jitter frequency: the input-to-output transfer is flat at 0 dB with a small peak near omega n and then falls; the VCO-to-output transfer rises at 40 dB per decade at low frequency and becomes flat at 0 dB above omega n.
blocks.caption: Jitter transfer in a type II PLL with $\zeta = 0.707$.

blocks.title: Static phase offset
blocks.text: A PLL at 100 MHz has $I_P = 100\ \mu\text{A}$, a 5% up/down mismatch, and reset pulses of 150 ps. Find the static phase offset.

blocks.title: Size of a dead zone
blocks.text: A pump needs pulses at least 50 ps wide to switch, and the PFD has no reset overlap. For a 1 GHz reference, what is the dead zone?
solution: $\phi_0 = 2\pi \times 50\text{ ps}/1\text{ ns} = 0.31\text{ rad}$ (18°): the VCO phase can wander that far uncorrected.

blocks.title: Jitter filtering numbers
blocks.text: A type II PLL has $\zeta = 1$. By how much is VCO phase noise at $\omega_n/10$ suppressed, and input jitter at $10\omega_n$ attenuated?
solution: VCO path at $\omega = 0.1\omega_n$: $|s^2/(s^2 + 2s\omega_n + \omega_n^2)| = 0.01/|0.99 + j0.2| = 0.0099$, about −40 dB.
Input path, $H = (2\zeta\omega_n s + \omega_n^2)/(\dots)$, at $10\omega_n$: $|1 + j20|/|{-99} + j20| = 20.0/101 = 0.198$, about −14 dB (only 20 dB/dec roll-off because of the zero).
blocks.answer: VCO noise −40 dB; input jitter −14 dB.

blocks.title: Charge sharing
blocks.text: Why does charge sharing disturb $V_{cont}$ even with perfectly matched currents and zero phase error, and why does bootstrapping cure it?
solution: With the switches open, the current sources drag their drain nodes to the rails. On closing, each node jumps to $V_{cont}$, but by unequal amounts (one is far from $V_{cont}$, one close), so the difference in charge comes from $C_P$.
If a buffer keeps both nodes at $V_{cont}$ while the switches are open, nothing moves when they close, so no charge is exchanged.
blocks.answer: Unequal jumps of the drain nodes; bootstrapping pre-sets them to $V_{cont}$.
